title: Iris and Velvy's Flying Hatbox
markdown:
In a snug nook beside a sparkling stream, where water lilies floated like sleepy green boats, lived Iris the duck. She was as cheerful as a summer morning, feathers the colour of sunshine, a quack that could make daisies nod and pebbles skip. Her best friend in the Whispering Woods was Velvy, a bat whose fur was as soft as a velvet curtain spun from moonbeams. His eyes gleamed like tiny friendly stars. Velvy did not so much fly as drift, and he hummed tunes that could calm a grumpy toad.

One blustery afternoon an official-looking envelope tumbled from the sky on a whirlwind’s whisper and landed at Iris’s webbed feet. Papery moonlight silk. A dewdrop seal. Inside, a card written in ink like starlight: You are cordially invited to the Queen of Moths’ Annual Moonpetal Ball.

“The Queen of Moths,” Velvy gasped, velvet ears twitching. “The most wonderful party in the woods. Music of captured moonlight. Decorations of spun-sugar cloud.”

The invitation had a small smudged corner, as if a mischievous gust had taken it the wrong way. The ball was tonight. If the card did not reach the Queen before the moon stood highest, her sparkle would dim, and the ball would feel a little less bright.

“We simply must return it,” Iris declared, chest puffed.

The Queen lived in a castle of gleaming moonbeams atop the tallest Whisperwind Willow. Too far for Iris to waddle. Velvy was far too small to carry both a duck and a precious invitation through a darkening sky.

They looked about. Floating just above the stream, not wetting a drop, bobbed a large round hatbox of sturdy patterned cardboard, as if it were a boat for giants that had decided water was optional.

“A floating hatbox,” Velvy whispered.

“It looks as if it could fly,” Iris quacked, and the hatbox lifted a little higher, caught by a playful breeze that seemed to giggle.

They climbed in with a hop and a flutter. The inside felt snug, like a warm nest lined with cotton, and smelled faintly of old hats and river wind. Iris set the invitation in a corner where it could not slide. The breeze pushed. The hatbox rose from reeds and lilies toward the rosy setting sun, wobbling once as if to say it had opinions, then settling.

Iris paddled her feet in the air and giggled. The stream became a silver ribbon. Her usual waddle-world shrank. Trees looked like giant green broccoli. A heron, very dignified, pretended not to see a duck in a hatbox. Velvy hummed, and the box drifted as steady as a sleepy cloud. They passed puffy white clouds like woolly sheep and birds sketching loops in the dusk. The first star came out early, nosy.

Then a sparkling cloud of tiny butterflies — wings like stained glass — giggled around them, the gossamer-winged sort that loved to play chase with anything that floated.

They swirled. They tickled Iris’s cheerful face and Velvy’s sensitive ears. The hatbox spun and wobbled. Powdered wing-dust tickled noses. Honeysuckle filled the air.

Iris tried to fan them away. The box tipped. The invitation nearly slid. She pinned it with a webbed foot and quacked a word that was not quite a word.

Velvy closed his eyes, breathed the sweet evening, and hummed his quiet tune louder, still soft, a lullaby on the wind. He had hummed toads calm. Butterflies, he hoped, were only toads with better clothes.

The butterflies stopped. They tilted their heads. The giggles quieted. They no longer wanted to tickle; they wanted to drift and listen. One landed on the brim of the hatbox as if it were a balcony. They swirled once more, a gentle rainbow, and with a last soft chime of laughter they rode the evening breeze away.

Iris nudged Velvy with her beak. “Your song saved us.”

The sky deepened to velvety purple. Shy stars came out. A radiant glow appeared in the distance: the Queen’s castle in the grandest willow, sparkling like a million tiny diamonds on dark velvet.

The hatbox landed with an almost silent bump on a luminous moonpetal outside the doors. A moth in a waistcoat of woven silver opened up, antennae quivering.

“Goodness. You’ve brought it back. We thought it lost forever.”

He ushered them into a hall of moths with wings like painted silk in every colour. Lanterns of captured dusk hung from willow ribs. The Queen, antennae like unfurling ferns, smiled so brightly she glowed brighter still.

“My dear friends. You have brought back our missing joy.” She dipped her head. “Stay. Dance. Dewdrop nectar, if you like.”

Iris and Velvy danced under moonlight, nibbled the sweetest dewdrops, and listened to music that sounded like the invitation had wanted all along to come home. The Queen’s sparkle stayed bright all evening. Later the hatbox floated them back, the moon painting silver paths on the water. The stars twinkled as if they had been in on the delivery from the start.
